newsitem.title: MALAWI: Malawi to begin trying backlog of murder cases.
newsitem.headline: Malawi to begin trying backlog of murder cases.

text.p: Malawian murder suspects, some of whom have been detained for over a decade, will start facing trial from June after British lawyers were called in to clear the backlog, a government official said on Friday.

Prosecutor Kamudoni Nyasulu said the three lawyers, funded by the Overseas Development Agency (ODA), had been reviewing a backlog of about 1,000 outstanding cases -- involving 1,442 accused -- to speed up the trials.
"In fact, one of them dates back to 1984," Nyasulu said in an interview with Reuters.
The reviews have already shown some 25 cases lacked sufficient evidence, he said, adding that he would close them and release the prisoners who had been incarcerated "for too long".
Other charges have been reduced to manslaughter with a sentence of life imprisonment.
Malawi laws provide for capital punishment by hanging for offences such as murder, rape and armed robbery.
The first 85 cases will go on trial next month, and Nyasulu said that by end of 1999 people on murder charges would be tried within one year of their arrest.

The Malawi government said murder suspects were detained without trial for such long periods due to insuffient funds to pay state lawyers. Most of the country's lawyers are in private practice where they earn more.

High Court Judge Dyress Kumange warned the government in Friday's edition of The Nation to end the unusually long delay in trying murder suspects and said the courts had not tried any murder cases in 1996.
"God will have his anger cast on us all if we delay the execution of justice ... and for unfairly prolonging incarceration of innocent suspects," he said.
